glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 23 warns the son against tables, riches, and wine that promise more than they give, and sets in their place a father’s plea for his whole heart and the LORD, the mighty Redeemer of the fatherless.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The chapter continues “the words of the wise” begun at 22:17, longer instructions in which a teacher speaks as a father to “my son.” Fresh appeals open at verses 15 and 19, and a closing poem portrays the drunkard.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “My son, give me your heart, And let your eyes observe my ways.” (Proverbs 23:26)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Much of Proverbs 23 happens at the table. The son sits before a ruler’s delicacies, then before a miser whose welcome hides the fact that “his heart is not with you” (23:7), then among “winebibbers” (23:20), and finally before a cup of wine that “sparkles” and “swirls around smoothly” (23:31). Each offer looks generous and hides a cost. Riches belong in the same company, for they “make themselves wings” (23:5). Here wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, looks like self-control: desire for food, money, or drink must be ruled, or it will rule the man.

Against these false hosts the chapter sets two who can be trusted. One is the LORD. The fatherless may have no kinsman left, yet “their Redeemer is mighty” (23:11). The other is the father, whose inmost being rejoices when his son’s “lips speak right things” (23:16). He calls the son away from envying sinners to zeal for the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, because “your hope will not be cut off” (23:18). His plea, “My son, give me your heart” (23:26), asks for what the ruler, the miser, the harlot, and the wine all try to capture. Through a human father’s voice, God’s own fatherly care asks for the whole heart.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 23:1–3 — Restraint at a Ruler’s Table

A guest at a ruler’s table is told to notice what is set before him and to curb his appetite as firmly as if he held a knife to his own throat, a deliberate overstatement. The rich dishes are “deceptive food” (23:3), served for the host’s purposes, so the man who craves them is easily used.

Proverbs 23:4–8 — Riches That Fly Away and the Miser’s Table

The son is told to stop wearing himself out for wealth, because riches sprout wings and are gone like an eagle into the sky; the warning is against making money the goal, not against honest work. A second table follows, where a stingy host urges his guest to eat while privately counting the cost, and the meal ends in nausea and wasted thanks.

Proverbs 23:9–12 — The Fatherless and Their Mighty Redeemer

Wise words spent on a fool are lost, because he will only despise them. The ancient landmark of 22:28 returns with orphans named as the ones robbed when it is moved, and the warning rests on the LORD Himself, their mighty Redeemer, who will take up their case; then the son is called once more to bring heart and ears to instruction.

Proverbs 23:13–18 — Correction, a Rejoicing Father, and a Sure Hope

Loving correction will not destroy a child but turns him from the path that ends in the grave, and these verses never license harshness, rage, or abuse. The father then speaks of the deep gladness a wise heart and upright speech give him, and he tells his son to trade envy of sinners for zeal for the fear of the LORD all day long, because the hope of the righteous will not be cut off.

Proverbs 23:19–28 — My Son, Give Me Your Heart

A second appeal asks the son to steer his heart in the right way, to keep clear of heavy drinkers and gluttons who end in rags, and to listen to the father who begot him and the mother who bore him, even in her old age. Truth is worth buying at any price and must never be sold, and the father asks for his son’s heart because the harlot is a pit that is easy to fall into and hard to climb out of.

Proverbs 23:29–35 — Who Has Woe?

Six questions about woe, quarrels, wounds, and bloodshot eyes find one answer: those who linger long at the wine. The poem moves from the wine’s red sparkle to its serpent’s bite, to a mind that sees strange things and a body reeling as if at sea, and it ends with the drinker, beaten and numb, already wanting another drink.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 23 treats appetite as a spiritual matter. Gluttony, the love of money, and drunkenness appear as one danger: a desire that promises satisfaction and then leaves a man sick, in rags, or enslaved (23:8, 21, 35). The drunkard’s portrait ends in his own words, so the reader hears how bondage talks, numb to its injuries. Scripture elsewhere shows that such bondage is not beyond God’s power to wash and set free (1 Corinthians 6:10–11).

The chapter also shows whose side God takes. An orphan whose boundary stone is moved has a mighty Redeemer, the kinsman-defender whom the rest of Scripture reveals fully in Christ. The rod of 23:13–14 belongs beside a father who delights in his son, so correction aims at rescue from the path of death and never excuses harshness, rage, or abuse.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Appetite under rule. Food, wealth, and wine all promise more than they give, and the wise restrain desire before it masters them (23:1–5, 20–21, 31–35).

What a host really thinks. The ruler’s food is deceptive (23:3) and the miser’s welcome is empty (23:6–8), for as a man “thinks in his heart, so is he” (23:7).

The LORD defends the vulnerable. The fatherless have a Redeemer who pleads their cause against anyone who takes their land (23:10–11).

A heart given to the father. A wise heart and right speech bring parents joy, and the father asks for the son’s heart and attention to his ways (23:15–16, 19, 24–26).

Hope instead of envy. Zeal for the fear of the LORD replaces envy of sinners, because the righteous have a future that will not fail (23:17–18).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Deceptive food (23:3). Rich food set out by a ruler for his own ends. The meal looks like favor, but it may be a lure, which is why the guest must “Consider carefully what is before you” (23:1).

Redeemer (23:11). The Hebrew go’el is the near kinsman who defends and restores a vulnerable relative. When the fatherless have no human kinsman to stand up for them, the LORD takes that role Himself (compare Job 19:25), and the canon reveals the Redeemer fully in Christ.

Hell (23:14). Here the word means Sheol, the grave and the realm of death. Correction rescues a child from the path of folly that leads there; it does not itself save the soul.

Hereafter (23:18). A future or outcome. The righteous have an end ahead of them that will not fail, while the sinner’s success has no future. Whether the word reaches beyond death is debated.

Harlot and seductress (23:27). Two names for the woman who ensnares men, pictured as “a deep pit” and “a narrow well” (23:27). The seductress is the same outsider to the young man’s home and to God’s ways met in chapters 5–7, and the son remains responsible for guarding his own heart (23:26).

sections.title: Riches That Fly Away and the Miser’s Table
The Fatherless and Their Mighty Redeemer
Correction, a Rejoicing Father, and a Sure Hope
My Son, Give Me Your Heart

1.brief: When the son sits down to eat with a ruler, he is told to consider carefully what is set before him. A great man’s table is not simply a meal; it is a setting that calls for watchfulness and discernment.
1.explain:
“When you sit down to eat with a ruler,”

The teacher pictures a young man invited to a powerful man’s table. In the ancient world, a meal with a ruler was an honor and an opportunity, and also a test. Rulers used hospitality to judge people, win their loyalty, and place them under obligation. The son might be there to seek favor, to serve, or simply because he was invited, but in every case the setting calls for care.

“Consider carefully what is before you;”

The command is to pay close attention. In Hebrew, “Consider carefully” repeats the verb for understanding, literally understanding, understand. The doubling presses the son to give the scene his full attention, so he must not eat absent-mindedly. “What is before you” is first of all the food spread on the table, and it also includes the whole situation: the host, his purposes, and what the meal might cost. A great man’s table is not simply a meal. The son must keep his wits about him, notice what is being offered and why, and not let the splendor of the occasion dull his judgment.
1.notes: The Hebrew phrase rendered “what is before you” can also mean who is before you. Most English versions, including the ESV and KJV, translate it as what, and both senses fit the scene.

2.brief: Put a knife to your throat if you are a man ruled by appetite. The startling picture is deliberate overstatement, calling for decisive self-restraint at a table where indulgence could cost a person dearly.
2.explain:
“And put a knife to your throat”

The language is startling on purpose. To “put a knife to your throat” is not a literal command. It is deliberate overstatement, a vivid way of saying, restrain yourself as decisively as if your life depended on it. The throat is where food goes down, and the picture is of cutting off appetite before it can carry a person away. Proverbs uses strong images like this to make a point stick.

“If you are a man given to appetite.”

The warning is aimed at the man “given to appetite,” someone whose desires easily take control. In Hebrew he is literally a master of appetite, though in truth his appetite masters him. At a ruler’s table, such a man is in danger. Rich food and fine wine can make him forget himself, say too much, or put himself in the host’s debt. The person who knows he has a weakness in this area must take especially firm action. Self-control is part of wisdom, and here it is applied to the most ordinary of desires.
2.notes: The word rendered “appetite” is the common Hebrew word often translated “soul.” It can name a person’s appetite or desire, and here it is the hunger that the knife at the throat is meant to restrain. The word for “throat” in the first line is a different Hebrew word.

3.brief: Craving the ruler’s delicacies is dangerous, because they are deceptive food. The rich dishes may be offered for the host’s own purposes, so the guest who wants them too much can be drawn in and used.
3.explain:
“Do not desire his delicacies,”

The “delicacies” are the choice dishes of a ruler’s table, rich food the son would rarely taste. The command is not merely “do not eat,” but “Do not desire.” The danger lies in craving them, letting the appetite fix on them until it governs his behavior.

“For they are deceptive food.”

The reason is that they are “deceptive food,” in Hebrew literally bread of lies. The meal looks like favor and generosity, but it may not be what it seems. A ruler might use a lavish table to flatter, to obligate, to loosen tongues, or to discover a guest’s weaknesses. The food is real, but the message it sends may be false. The son who wants the delicacies too much can be drawn in and used. Wisdom sees past the surface of an offer to the purpose behind it. This is the first of several tables in the chapter where the food is not what it appears to be, and the miser’s table follows in 23:6–8.

4.brief: Do not wear yourself out trying to get rich; have the good sense to stop. Diligent work is commended throughout Proverbs, but exhausting oneself to make riches the goal is folly.
4.explain:
“Do not overwork to be rich;”

The second instruction moves from food to money. The son must not “overwork to be rich,” wearing himself out in the pursuit of wealth. Proverbs praises hard work throughout, so this is not a warning against diligence. The problem is making riches the goal and spending one’s strength, health, and attention chasing them. A person can work hard for good reasons, to provide for his family and to give to others, without exhausting himself for wealth as an end in itself.

“Because of your own understanding, cease!”

The second line calls the son to stop, and the NKJV ties that stopping to his “own understanding.” The most likely sense is that he should have the good sense to quit, using the discernment he has to recognize that the endless pursuit of wealth is folly. Money is a useful tool, but it is not everything, and the wise person knows when enough is enough. God promises to meet needs. He does not promise to make everyone rich, and the person who wears himself out for riches has misunderstood what life is for.
4.notes: The second line is difficult and has been read in two ways. The NKJV, ESV, and NLT understand it as using good sense to stop. The NASB (1995) reads it as a command to cease from one’s consideration of wealth, that is, to stop thinking about it. The KJV reads it as a command to cease from one’s own wisdom, that is, to stop relying on one’s own cleverness to get rich, which recalls “lean not on your own understanding” (3:5).

5.brief: Will you fix your eyes on something that is here and then gone? Riches sprout wings and fly off like an eagle into the sky, so setting the heart on them means trusting what will not stay.
5.explain:
“Will you set your eyes on that which is not?”

The teacher asks a question that exposes the folly of chasing wealth. To “set your eyes on” something is to fix your attention and desire on it. Riches are “that which is not,” something that seems solid but has no lasting substance. The question asks whether the son really wants to give his heart to something that can disappear in a moment.

“For riches certainly make themselves wings;”

The answer comes in a striking image. Riches “make themselves wings,” as if money could suddenly sprout feathers. One day it is there, and the next it has flown. Markets fail, thieves steal, disasters strike, and wealth is gone. The word “certainly” stresses that this is no rare accident. It is the nature of riches.

“They fly away like an eagle toward heaven.”

The picture is completed. Like an eagle soaring upward until it is out of sight, wealth flies away beyond recovery. An eagle in flight cannot be caught or called back. Setting the heart on riches means trusting what will not stay. The saying does not condemn possessions or honest gain, but it warns against making them the anchor of life.

6.brief: The son should not eat the food of a stingy man or long for his fine dishes. After the ruler’s table comes the miser’s table, another meal where the food is not what it seems.
6.explain:
“Do not eat the bread of a miser,”

After the ruler’s table comes another meal. In Hebrew the “miser” is literally a man with an evil eye, the opposite of the “generous eye” praised in 22:9. He is stingy, grudging, and always counting the cost. The son is told not to eat his “bread,” not to accept his hospitality.

“Nor desire his delicacies;”

As at the ruler’s table, the warning includes desire. The miser may set out fine dishes, but the son should not want them. The repetition of “desire his delicacies” from 23:3 links the two scenes. In both, the food is not what it seems, and the person who craves it walks into an uncomfortable trap. The miser’s food comes with strings: resentment, calculation, and an expectation of return. The next verses explain why.
6.notes: The Hebrew behind “miser” is literally one who is evil of eye, the same expression translated “evil eye” in 28:22, where such a man “hastens after riches” (28:22).

7.brief: As he calculates in his heart, so he really is. He says, “Eat and drink!” but his heart is not with you, so his hospitality is a show that hides a grudging, counting spirit.
7.explain:
“For as he thinks in his heart, so is he.”

The key to the miser is what goes on inside him. “As he thinks in his heart, so is he” means that his true character is found in his private calculations, not in his public words. The context suggests a man who is inwardly counting every bite his guest takes. His real self is the grudging man inside, whatever face he shows outside.

“Eat and drink!” he says to you,

Outwardly he plays the generous host. He says, “Eat and drink!” and urges his guest to enjoy the meal. The words sound warm and welcoming, but they do not match his heart.

“But his heart is not with you.”

The truth is that “his heart is not with you.” His hospitality is a show. He resents what the guest eats and keeps a mental account of what it costs him. Eating at such a table puts the son in an awkward and false position, enjoying what is given without real goodwill. The verse teaches the son to look past words to the heart, and to recognize that real generosity is a matter of the heart, not just the hand.
7.notes:
The Hebrew verb translated “thinks” appears only here in the Old Testament, and its sense has been debated. It is usually understood as calculating or reckoning, and several modern versions take it that way; the ESV has “calculating,” and the NLT speaks of thinking about the cost. That sense fits the miser who counts what his guest eats. The NKJV and KJV keep the more general “thinks.”

The line is often quoted on its own as a statement about thought determining character. In context it describes the miser whose inward calculation reveals what he really is.

8.brief: The bite you have eaten you will vomit up, and your pleasant words of thanks will be wasted. Discovering the host’s real attitude turns the meal sour, and the polite conversation spent on him comes to nothing.
8.explain:
“The morsel you have eaten, you will vomit up,”

The end of the meal is unpleasant. The “morsel” is the small bite the guest ate, and he “will vomit up” what he has eaten. The language may describe real sickness, or it may picture the disgust a guest feels when he realizes his host begrudged every mouthful. Either way, what seemed like a pleasant meal turns sour. Food eaten at a grudging table does not sit well.

“And waste your pleasant words.”

The “pleasant words” are the polite conversation and thanks the guest offered his host. They are wasted, spent on a man who never meant his welcome. The guest tried to be gracious, but his kindness was poured out on someone with no goodwill toward him. The lesson is to be discerning about whose hospitality one accepts. Some offers are worth refusing, because what is given with a grudging heart costs more than it is worth.

9.brief: Speaking wisdom in the hearing of a fool is wasted, because he will scorn the wisdom of your words. Some people will only despise good counsel, and wisdom knows when to keep silent.
9.explain:
“Do not speak in the hearing of a fool,”

The “fool” in Proverbs is not someone who lacks intelligence. He is morally deficient, someone who despises wisdom and instruction. The son is told not to “speak in the hearing of” such a person, meaning not to pour out wise counsel on someone who will not receive it.

“For he will despise the wisdom of your words.”

The reason is that the fool “will despise the wisdom of your words.” He will not just ignore them; he will treat them with contempt. Wise words spent on a fool are wasted and may even provoke him. Jesus gave a similar warning about casting pearls before swine in Matthew 7:6. Wisdom includes knowing when to speak and when to keep silent. That is not a refusal to love the fool. Some people are not ready to listen, and pressing wise words on them may only draw out their contempt. Proverbs elsewhere shows that there are times to answer a fool and times not to, as 26:4–5 shows, and discerning which is which is itself part of wisdom.

10.brief: Do not move the ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless. Repeating 22:28, the warning now names the most vulnerable victims, orphans with no one to protect their family land.
10.explain:
“Do not remove the ancient landmark,”

The command repeats 22:28. The “ancient landmark” is the boundary stone that marked a family’s inherited land, set long ago and protected by the law of Moses in Deuteronomy 19:14. Moving it was a quiet way to steal land.

“Nor enter the fields of the fatherless;”

This time the warning names the most likely victims. The “fatherless” were orphans with no father to defend their family’s land. To “enter” their fields was to encroach on them, taking land a strip at a time, knowing no one would object. The fatherless had no one to protect them and no power to resist. The land-grabber assumed that no one would come to their defense. The command forbids taking advantage of the most vulnerable, and God’s law repeatedly singles out the fatherless for His special protection: “He administers justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18).

11.brief: Their Redeemer is mighty, and He will plead their case against you. The fatherless may have no human kinsman to defend them, but the LORD Himself takes up that role, the Redeemer whom the rest of Scripture reveals fully in Christ.
11.explain:
“For their Redeemer is mighty;”

The reason for the command is that the fatherless are not alone. They have a “Redeemer.” In Israel the redeemer was the nearest kinsman, the relative whose duty was to buy back family land that had been sold, to free a relative who had fallen into servitude, and to defend the cause of a family member who could not defend himself, as Leviticus 25:25 describes. Boaz acted as redeemer for Ruth and Naomi. The orphan whose land is being stolen seems to have no such kinsman. The verse says he does, and his Redeemer “is mighty.” The LORD Himself takes up the role of next of kin for those who have no one else.

“He will plead their cause against you.”

The Redeemer acts as advocate. He “will plead their cause against you,” taking the case of the fatherless to court and arguing it against the one who wronged them. The same language described the LORD’s defense of the poor in 22:23. The person who moves an orphan’s boundary stone has not escaped notice. He has made an enemy of God. Job confessed, “For I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25), and the rest of Scripture reveals the Redeemer fully in Christ, who became our kinsman by sharing our flesh and who defends those who have no other defender.
11.notes:
“Redeemer” translates the Hebrew go’el, the kinsman-redeemer of Leviticus 25 and the Book of Ruth. The word names the close relative whose family duty was to buy back lost land, free a relative from servitude, and take up his cause. Applied to the LORD here, it means that the fatherless, who have no such relative, have God Himself acting as their next of kin.

Jeremiah uses closely similar words of the LORD’s defense of His exiled people: “Their Redeemer is strong; The LORD of hosts is His name. He will thoroughly plead their case” (Jeremiah 50:34).

12.brief: Apply your heart to instruction and your ears to words of knowledge. Between warnings, the call to listen returns, for wisdom must be received with both heart and ear.
12.explain:
“Apply your heart to instruction,”

Between warnings, the call to listen returns, much like the opening call of the collection in 22:17. “Apply your heart” means to bring the whole inner person to the task of learning. “Instruction” is discipline and training, the teaching that corrects and forms a person. The son is to set his heart on receiving it.

“And your ears to words of knowledge.”

The second line adds the ears. Wisdom must be received with both heart and ear: the ear hears the words, and the heart takes them in and acts on them. This brief call reminds the son that the warnings he is hearing are not random rules. They are instruction from a teacher who wants him to grow wise. It also prepares for the next section, where instruction takes the form of a parent’s correction (23:13–14).
12.notes: The Hebrew word for “instruction” here, a word for discipline and training, is the same word translated “correction” in 23:13, which links the call to listen with the saying on discipline that follows.

13.brief: Correction is not to be held back from a child, for if you discipline him with the rod, he will not die. Loving correction will not destroy a child, whereas the lack of it may lead him toward ruin; the verse never justifies harshness, rage, or abuse.
13.explain:
“Do not withhold correction from a child,”

The command is to give correction and not hold it back. In Hebrew, “correction” is the same word translated “instruction” in 23:12, and it covers the whole work of training, teaching, and correcting a child. A parent may hold back out of busyness, a wish to avoid conflict, or a mistaken idea of kindness. The verse says that is not love. The book has already said, “he who loves him disciplines him promptly” (13:24).

“For if you beat him with a rod, he will not die.”

The second line reassures the parent: correction with the rod “will not” kill the child. Loving correction does not destroy a child, while the lack of it may lead him toward ruin. Parents who fear that correcting their child will harm him are told that the greater harm lies in neglecting it. The rod is the tool of correction in its biblical setting, and it includes physical correction. Yet the verse gives no license for harshness. As at 13:24 and 22:15, discipline in Proverbs is restorative. It is given calmly and with love, never in rage or frustration, and it never justifies abuse. Its aim is to turn the child from a harmful course toward what is right.
13.notes: Where the NKJV and KJV have “beat,” the ESV and the NASB (1995) have “strike.” The Hebrew verb is the common word for striking or hitting, used of blows of every kind.

14.brief: By correcting him with the rod you will rescue his soul from hell, here meaning the grave and the realm of death. Discipline turns a child from the path of folly that ends in death; it does not itself save the soul.
14.explain:
“You shall beat him with a rod,”

The first line restates the parent’s responsibility. Correction is to be given and not avoided. The repetition from 23:13 underlines the duty without making it a call to severity. It asks for the faithful correction that flows from love and aims at the child’s good.

“And deliver his soul from hell.”

The goal is rescue. “Hell” here translates the Hebrew word Sheol, the grave and the realm of death. To “deliver his soul” is to snatch his life away from the road that ends there. Proverbs repeatedly shows folly as a path that leads to death, “Descending to the chambers of death” (7:27), and loving correction turns a child off that path before it is too late. The verse does not mean that physical discipline saves a child’s soul or earns eternal life; salvation is God’s work. What correction does is pull a young person back from the way of folly and point him toward the way of life. It is an act of rescue, and like the book’s other sayings it describes what correction aims at, not a guarantee of how every child will turn out.
14.notes: The Hebrew word behind “hell” is Sheol, the Old Testament name for the realm of the dead. The ESV and the NASB (1995) keep “Sheol,” and the NLT renders it “death.”

15.brief: My son, if your heart is wise, my own heart will rejoice. The father opens a fresh appeal by telling the son how much his wisdom means to him personally.
15.explain:
“My son, if your heart is wise,”

A fresh appeal begins with “My son.” The father speaks warmly and personally. His concern is the son’s “heart,” the inner person, and he hopes that heart will be “wise.” Wisdom here is more than knowledge in the head. It is skill for living, rooted in the heart.

“My heart will rejoice—indeed, I myself;”

The father’s response is joy. “My heart will rejoice” answers “your heart” in the first line, so a wise heart in the son produces a glad heart in the father. The added words “indeed, I myself” make it emphatic and personal. The father is not merely pleased with a well-behaved child; he himself is glad. Solomon’s collection opened on the same note: “A wise son makes a glad father” (10:1). By beginning this appeal with his own delight rather than with a threat, the father gives the son a reason to listen that is stronger than fear.

16.brief: My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right. The father’s joy goes deep, and it is the son’s upright speech, the fruit of a wise heart, that brings it.
16.explain:
“Yes, my inmost being will rejoice”

The father’s joy goes deeper still. “My inmost being” stands for the depths of a person, the seat of the most personal feelings. His gladness is not polite approval. It reaches the core of who he is.

“When your lips speak right things.”

What brings this joy is the son’s speech, “When your lips speak right things.” Upright speech is the fruit of a wise heart, so the heart of 23:15 shows itself through the lips of 23:16. Later in the chapter the drunkard’s heart “will utter perverse things” (23:33), and the contrast is plain. Words reveal what is inside, and a father rejoices when his son’s words are right.
16.notes: “Inmost being” is literally kidneys, which the KJV renders “reins.” In Hebrew idiom the kidneys represent the deepest emotions and thoughts.

17.brief: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but be zealous for the fear of the LORD all day long. Instead of looking enviously at those who seem to prosper through sin, the son is to keep his passion fixed on a right view of God.
17.explain:
“Do not let your heart envy sinners,”

The son might look at sinners who seem to prosper and feel envy. They enjoy comfort, success, and freedom from the restraints he lives under. Envy begins in the heart, and the father warns against letting it take root. Envy of the wicked is a recurring danger in the words of the wise (24:1, 19), because it can lead a person to leave the right path in order to imitate those who seem to be getting ahead.

“But be zealous for the fear of the LORD all the day;”

In place of envy, the son is to be zealous for “the fear of the LORD,” a right view of God that produces awe, trust, and obedience. Zeal is passionate devotion, and it is to last “all the day,” without interruption. The cure for envy is more than ceasing to want what sinners have. It is setting the heart’s passion on something better. When a person sees God rightly, the prosperity of sinners loses its glitter.
17.notes: The Hebrew verb for “envy” in the first line can also mean to be zealous, and it carries over into the second line, which has no verb of its own. The NKJV brings this out with “be zealous,” while the ESV and NLT supply “continue.” The one verb thus names both the wrong passion and the right one.

18.brief: There is surely a future, and your hope will not be cut off. The reason not to envy sinners is that the righteous have an outcome ahead of them that will not fail, while the sinner’s prosperity has no future (compare 24:14).
18.explain:
“For surely there is a hereafter,”

The reason not to envy sinners is that the righteous have a future. “Hereafter” translates a Hebrew word meaning an end or a future outcome. The sinner’s prosperity has no lasting future, but the righteous person’s story is heading toward a good end. The word does not by itself describe life after death, and this verse cannot carry a doctrine of the afterlife on its own. It does point the son past present appearances to the outcome God holds.

“And your hope will not be cut off.”

The son’s “hope,” his expectation of good from God, “will not be cut off.” It will not be destroyed or disappointed. The promise returns almost word for word in 24:14, and the contrast is stated outright soon after: “there will be no prospect for the evil man” (24:20). The wise person can wait patiently, because the God he fears holds his future, and the rest of Scripture shows that this hope reaches beyond the grave.
18.notes: The Hebrew word rendered “hereafter” is the same word translated “prospect” in 24:14 and 24:20 and “At the last” in 23:32. The KJV renders it “an end,” with “reward” in the margin, and the ESV and NASB have “future.”

19.brief: Listen, my son, and be wise, and keep your heart on the right path. A new appeal begins, calling the son to steer his heart, the source of his choices, along the way of wisdom.
19.explain:
“Hear, my son, and be wise;”

A new appeal begins with “my son.” The father calls for hearing that leads to wisdom. Listening is the first step, and the goal is to “be wise,” to become a person whose life is ordered by God’s way.

“And guide your heart in the way.”

The son must “guide” his “heart,” steering the inner person as a traveler keeps to the road. “The way” is the path of wisdom that runs through the whole book. The heart is the source of a person’s choices, so keeping it on the right path keeps the whole life there. The father said in the prologue, “Keep your heart with all diligence, For out of it spring the issues of life” (4:23). The next verses show what the heart must be steered away from: drunkenness and gluttony.

20.brief: The son is told not to join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat. He is warned not only against overindulgence but against the company of those who live for it.
20.explain:
“Do not mix with winebibbers,”

“Winebibbers” are heavy drinkers, people who drink wine to excess. To “mix with” them is to join their company and share their way of life. The warning concerns companions as well as conduct, because the people a person spends time with influence what he becomes.

“Or with gluttonous eaters of meat;”

The second group is the gluttons, people who gorge themselves on meat. Meat was a luxury in Israel, usually eaten at feasts, so these are people who live for indulgence. Heavy drinking and gluttony go together as a life given over to appetite. The son is warned not only against overindulging himself but against the company of those who make indulgence a way of life.
20.notes: The Hebrew words behind “winebibbers” and “gluttonous” here, and “drunkard” and “glutton” in 23:21, are the pair used of the rebellious son in the law: “he is a glutton and a drunkard” (Deuteronomy 21:20).

21.brief: The drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and drowsiness will dress a man in rags. A life given over to appetite ends in sluggish ruin and want.
21.explain:
“For the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty,”

The reason for the warning is practical. “The drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty.” A life given to appetite consumes money, time, and health. What is spent on excess cannot be spent on what lasts, and the habits of indulgence wear down a person’s ability to work.

“And drowsiness will clothe a man with rags.”

“Drowsiness” is the sluggish stupor that follows heavy eating and drinking, and the laziness that grows out of a life of indulgence. It “will clothe a man with rags.” The picture is of someone whose clothes have worn through and who cannot afford to replace them. The man who dressed for feasts ends in rags. Proverbs describes the general outcome of such a life. It does not say that every poor person came to poverty this way.

22.brief: Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not look down on your mother when she is old. Honor for parents does not end when a son grows up or when they grow frail.
22.explain:
“Listen to your father who begot you,”

The father reminds the son of the bond between them. He is “your father who begot you,” the one who gave him life, and that relationship gives his counsel weight. A grown son may think he has outgrown his father’s advice, but the command is to keep listening.

“And do not despise your mother when she is old.”

The mother is honored alongside the father. The son must not “despise” her, treating her with contempt or neglect, “when she is old.” Age can make parents seem slow, weak, or out of touch, and it is easy for a grown child to look down on them. The command forbids it. Honor for parents does not end when a son becomes independent or when they grow frail. The verse applies the commandment “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12) to the later years of life, when honor often costs the most.

23.brief: Buy the truth and do not sell it, along with wisdom, instruction, and understanding. Truth is worth any price to acquire, and nothing should ever tempt a person to trade it away.
23.explain:
“Buy the truth, and do not sell it,”

The language is commercial. To “Buy the truth” is to acquire it at whatever cost: effort, time, humility, and the surrender of comfortable lies. Truth is worth paying for. Once acquired, it must never be sold. No price, whether money, popularity, advantage, or pleasure, is worth trading truth away. The command fits a chapter full of offers that look attractive but deceive, from the ruler’s “deceptive food” (23:3) to the cup that “bites like a serpent” (23:32).

“Also wisdom and instruction and understanding.”

The second line adds three more treasures to buy: “wisdom,” skill for living; “instruction,” the training and correction that form character; and “understanding,” the ability to see clearly and discern. With truth, these are the real riches of the wise. The prologue said the same: “Therefore get wisdom. And in all your getting, get understanding” (4:7). Unlike the riches that fly away in 23:5, these last.

24.brief: The father of a righteous son will greatly rejoice, and whoever has a wise child will delight in him. A child’s wisdom and righteousness are a parent’s deepest joy.
24.explain:
“The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice,”

The father returns to the theme of a parent’s joy. A father whose son is “righteous,” living rightly before God, “will greatly rejoice.” No achievement or fortune gives a parent such deep joy as a child who walks with God.

“And he who begets a wise child will delight in him.”

The second line repeats the thought. The one who “begets a wise child” will “delight in him.” Wisdom and righteousness belong together in Proverbs, and both bring parents deep gladness. This joy is more than pride in a successful child. It is delight in who the child has become. The verse also tells the son something he may not realize: his choices touch his parents’ happiness more than he knows.
24.notes: The Hebrew of the first line repeats the verb for rejoicing, which the NKJV conveys with “greatly rejoice.”

25.brief: Let your father and mother be glad, and let her who bore you rejoice. The son is urged to give his parents the joy just described, with special mention of his mother.
25.explain:
“Let your father and your mother be glad,”

The father now urges the son to give his parents this joy. “Let your father and your mother be glad” is both a wish and a call to action. The son can make his parents glad by choosing wisdom and righteousness. Both parents are named, as in 23:22.

“And let her who bore you rejoice.”

The mother receives special mention. “Her who bore you” recalls the pain and love of childbirth, and her joy is singled out, just as the book elsewhere says that a foolish son is “bitterness to her who bore him” (17:25). The son who lives wisely repays something of what his mother gave. This prepares for the heart of the appeal in 23:26.

26.brief: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways. The father asks for the whole inner person and close attention to how he lives, an obedience that comes from the heart; at a deeper level, his appeal carries the voice of God’s fatherly care calling for the whole heart.
26.explain:
“My son, give me your heart,”

This is the center of the father’s appeal. He asks for his son’s “heart,” the whole inner person: thoughts, desires, will, and affections. He is asking for more than outward obedience. He wants the son’s heart given to him, so that the son wants what the father wants and trusts his guidance. Everything else in the chapter tries to capture the son’s heart: the ruler’s delicacies, riches, the miser’s table, the harlot, and the wine. The father asks for it first.

“And let your eyes observe my ways.”

The second line asks for attention to the father’s example. The son’s eyes are to “observe my ways,” watching how his father lives and learning from it. Instruction comes through a life lived before the child as well as through words, and the father offers his own conduct as a pattern.

At a deeper level, the father’s voice carries the voice of God’s fatherly care. The God who made the son and loves him asks the same thing: the whole heart, and eyes fixed on His ways. That request stands beneath the instructions of Proverbs, and it answers the many voices competing for the heart.
26.notes: The Hebrew text preserves two readings of the verb in the second line. The letters written in the text give a verb meaning to delight in or be pleased with. A note in the margin of Hebrew Bibles directs the reader to a different verb meaning to keep, watch, or observe. The NKJV, ESV, and KJV follow the margin reading, while the NASB (1995) and NLT follow the written text with “delight.” With “observe,” the father asks the son to watch his conduct and keep to it; with “delight,” he asks the son to take pleasure in the way his father lives. Either way the request follows from a heart given to the father.

27.brief: A harlot is a deep pit, and a seductress a narrow well. Both images describe a trap that is easy to fall into and nearly impossible to climb out of, which is why the son must guard his heart (verse 26).
27.explain:
“For a harlot is a deep pit,”

The reason for giving the father the heart follows at once. A “harlot,” a prostitute, “is a deep pit.” Like the pits dug to trap animals, she is easy to fall into and almost impossible to climb out of. The same image described the immoral woman’s mouth in 22:14.

“And a seductress is a narrow well.”

The second line adds the “seductress,” the outsider woman of chapters 5–7 who draws a young man away from his own home and from God’s ways. She is “a narrow well,” a shaft too tight to climb out of once a person has fallen in. Both images picture a trap from which escape is extremely hard. The verse does not portray women as the danger. It describes the particular snare of sexual sin, and it leaves the son responsible for guarding his own heart, as 23:26 has just urged.

28.brief: She lies in wait like a robber for her prey and increases the number of unfaithful men. Her danger is active, not passive; she hunts, and those she catches add to the ranks of the faithless.
28.explain:
“She also lies in wait as for a victim,”

The danger is active. She “lies in wait,” like a hunter or a bandit hiding beside the road. The young man may think he is the one pursuing her, but he is the one being hunted. Proverbs 7 showed the same scene, with the woman “Lurking at every corner” (7:12) and catching the young man as he passed.

“And increases the unfaithful among men.”

Her success adds to “the unfaithful among men.” Each man she catches becomes unfaithful to his wife, to his family, and to God. She does more than ruin individuals; she multiplies faithlessness in the community. The son who gives his heart to his father guards himself against becoming one of them. For those who have already fallen, Proverbs holds out mercy: “whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (28:13).
28.notes: The Hebrew word behind “as for a victim” has been understood in two ways, as prey or as a robber. The NKJV and KJV take it as prey, picturing the man she catches, while the ESV, the NASB (1995), and the NLT read “robber,” picturing the woman herself as the one lying in ambush. The KJV margin also offers the robber reading.

29.brief: Who has woe and sorrow, quarrels and complaints, wounds for no reason and bloodshot eyes? The string of questions builds a vivid picture of misery before naming its cause.
29.explain:
“Who has woe? Who has sorrow?”

The poem opens with a string of questions, like a riddle. “Woe” is a cry of pain, and “sorrow” is grief or misery. The teacher asks who suffers these things and lets the questions build before he gives the answer.

“Who has contentions? Who has complaints?”

The questions move from inner misery to trouble with others. “Contentions” are quarrels and fights, and “complaints” are the grumbling and grievances that follow them. The drinker’s life is full of conflict.

“Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes?”

“Wounds without cause” are injuries from brawls and falls that never needed to happen, bruises the drinker cannot even explain. “Redness of eyes” describes the bloodshot eyes of a man who has been drinking. Six questions build a vivid picture: pain, grief, quarrels, complaints, needless injuries, and bloodshot eyes. Together they describe a whole life damaged in body, in relationships, and in soul. The answer comes in 23:30.
29.notes: Proverbs 23:29–35 is a self-contained poem, the fullest portrait of drunkenness in the book. It opens with questions (23:29), names the cause (23:30), gives a warning (23:31–32), describes the effects (23:33–34), and ends in the drinker’s own words (23:35).

30.brief: The answer comes: those who linger long over wine and go looking for mixed drink. The pain of the previous verse belongs to people who make drinking a pursuit.
30.explain:
“Those who linger long at the wine,”

The answer is given. These troubles belong to “Those who linger long at the wine.” They are not people who drink a cup with a meal. They stay late, drink long, and make drinking an occupation.

“Those who go in search of mixed wine.”

They also “go in search of mixed wine,” wine that has been mixed and prepared for drinking. These are people who seek drink out instead of merely accepting a cup when it is offered. Drinking has become a pursuit, and the misery listed in 23:29 belongs to people whose lives revolve around it.
30.notes:
Isaiah condemns the same pursuit: “Woe to men mighty at drinking wine, Woe to men valiant for mixing intoxicating drink” (Isaiah 5:22).

The Hebrew word behind “mixed wine” comes from the same root as the verb for mixing in Wisdom’s preparation of her banquet, “She has mixed her wine” (9:2), where the table leads to life.

31.brief: Do not gaze at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. The warning targets the allure itself, the inviting look and smooth taste that draw a person in.
31.explain:
“Do not look on the wine when it is red,”

The poem now turns to warning. The danger starts with the eyes, with gazing at the wine and being drawn by its rich color. The warning targets the allure, the attraction that pulls a person in before he has taken a sip.

“When it sparkles in the cup,”

The wine “sparkles in the cup,” catching the light and looking lovely. The description is honest. Wine is attractive, and the teacher does not pretend otherwise. That is exactly why it is dangerous.

“When it swirls around smoothly;”

It “swirls around smoothly,” moving in the cup and going down easily. Every sense is engaged: the color, the sparkle, the smooth taste. This is how temptation works. It looks good, feels good, and goes down easily. Scripture elsewhere counts wine among God’s gifts, as in Psalm 104:15. What this verse warns against is the gazing and longing that lead to the bondage pictured in 23:32–35, and the book has already said that “whoever is led astray by it is not wise” (20:1).
31.notes:
The Hebrew word rendered “smoothly” means what is level, straight, or upright, and it is the word translated “right things” in 23:16. The son’s lips speak what is upright, while the wine merely goes down “smoothly.”

The ESV, NASB, and NLT render the last line as the wine going down smoothly. A closely similar Hebrew expression appears in Song of Solomon 7:9, “The wine goes down smoothly” (Song of Solomon 7:9).

32.brief: In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like a viper. What looked so pleasant turns out to be poisonous, and its harm arrives after the pleasure has passed.
32.explain:
“At the last it bites like a serpent,”

The pleasant beginning has a bitter end. “At the last,” when the pleasure has passed, the wine “bites like a serpent.” What looked so attractive turns out to be poisonous. The harm comes after the enjoyment, which is why the drinker does not see it coming.

“And stings like a viper.”

The second line repeats the image with a “viper,” a poisonous snake whose sting brings pain, sickness, and possibly death. Wine abused works like venom on the body, the mind, relationships, and the soul. The contrast between 23:31 and 23:32 is the contrast between how sin looks at the beginning and what it does at the end. Proverbs traces the same pattern in the immoral woman, whose lips “drip honey” and yet “in the end she is bitter as wormwood” (5:3–4).

33.brief: Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart will speak twisted things. Drunkenness distorts both perception and speech, so the drinker no longer sees or says what is true.
33.explain:
“Your eyes will see strange things,”

The poem now describes the drinker’s experience directly, addressing him as “you.” His eyes “will see strange things”: distorted perceptions, confusion, perhaps hallucinations. He can no longer see the world as it is.

“And your heart will utter perverse things.”

His heart “will utter perverse things.” Twisted, foolish, or shameful words come out of him. Drunkenness distorts both perception and speech, so the drinker no longer sees or says what is true. The son whose lips “speak right things” (23:16) stands in contrast. A wise heart produces right speech, while the drunken heart pours out what is twisted. Wine removes restraint and exposes what is inside, and it makes a person say what he would never say sober.
33.notes: The Hebrew word translated “strange things” is a plural form that can also mean strange women, and the KJV renders it “strange women.” The same plural word stands behind “immoral woman” in 22:14. Most modern versions agree with the NKJV’s “strange things.”

34.brief: You will be like someone lying down in the middle of the sea, or sleeping at the top of a ship’s mast. The pictures capture the dizziness and danger of drunkenness, as if a person were reeling with every wave.
34.explain:
“Yes, you will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea,”

The drinker’s condition is compared to lying down “in the midst of the sea.” The picture is of someone trying to sleep on the open water, rocked by the waves, dizzy and unsteady, and in real danger of drowning. He cannot find solid ground.

“Or like one who lies at the top of the mast, saying:”

The second picture is even more precarious: lying “at the top of the mast,” high above the deck of a ship and swaying with every roll. No one in his right mind would sleep there. Both images capture the dizziness, the loss of balance, and the danger of drunkenness, along with the drinker’s strange indifference to his own peril. The word “saying” introduces his own words in 23:35.

35.brief: The drinker boasts that the blows did not hurt and he never felt them, then asks, “When shall I awake, that I may seek another drink?” The portrait ends in his own words, numb to harm and bound to the very thing that is ruining him, yet 1 Corinthians 6:10–11 shows that such bondage is not beyond God’s power to wash and set free.
35.explain:
“They have struck me, but I was not hurt;”

Now the drinker speaks. He boasts that he was struck and not hurt. He has been in a fight or beaten, but the drink numbed him to the pain, and he takes his numbness as proof that nothing is wrong.

“They have beaten me, but I did not feel it.”

He says it again: he was beaten and did not feel it. The drink has dulled his senses so that he cannot feel the harm being done to him. The numbness that seems like a mercy is itself part of the danger.

“When shall I awake, that I may seek another drink?”

The poem ends with his question. Bruised and dazed, his first thought on waking is to drink again. This is the voice of bondage. He is enslaved to the very thing that is ruining him. The portrait is sober and true, and it is given so that the son will see where the road leads before he takes it.

It is not the final word on those who are enslaved. Paul names drunkards among those who will not inherit the kingdom of God, and then he writes, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). No bondage is beyond God’s power to wash and set free.
